title: GoldMining Appoints Martin Dumont as VP, Corporate Development and Investor Relations
summary: GoldMining Inc. is a public mineral exploration company advancing gold-copper projects in the Americas through exploration, strategic investments, and partnerships.
body_text: GoldMining Appoints Martin Dumont as VP, Corporate Development and Investor Relations Share: Vancouver, British Columbia – January 22, 2026 – GoldMining Inc. (the " Company " or " GoldMining ") (TSX: GOLD; NYSE American: GLDG) is pleased to announce the appointment of Martin Dumont as Vice President, Corporate Development & Investor Relations. Alastair Still, President & Chief Executive Officer of GoldMining commented: “We are pleased to welcome Martin to the GoldMining team. His mining industry experience across corporate development, capital markets, and investor relations within the gold sector will play a key role as we continue to advance our portfolio and pursue value-accretive opportunities. Martin’s perspective and track record strengthen our ability to communicate our strategy and execute on initiatives that support long-term shareholder value.” Martin Dumont commented: “I am excited to join GoldMining at a pivotal stage in the Company’s growth. GoldMining has assembled a unique portfolio of high-quality gold and gold-copper assets across the Americas, offering multiple pathways to value creation. I look forward to working closely with the management team to advance strategic initiatives, strengthen investor engagement, and help unlock the full value of the Company’s assets for shareholders.” Mr. Dumont is an experienced finance professional in the metals and mining sector with a background in corporate development, equity research, investor relations, and operations finance. Prior to joining GoldMining, Mr. Dumont held a senior role in corporate development at Sandstorm Gold Royalties, where he focused on streaming and royalty transactions as well as corporate M&A. Prior to joining Sandstorm, Mr. Dumont was an equity research associate at BMO Capital Markets covering senior gold, copper, and royalty companies, and held progressively senior positions in investor relations and operations finance at IAMGOLD Corporation. Mr. Dumont earned a Bachelor of Business Administration from the University of Guelph and is a Chartered Professional Accountant (CPA, CA). About GoldMining Inc. GoldMining Inc. is a public mineral exploration company focused on acquiring and developing gold assets in the Americas. Through its disciplined acquisition strategy, GoldMining now controls a diversified portfolio of resource-stage gold and gold-copper projects in Canada, the U.S.A., Brazil, Colombia, and Peru. The Company also owns approximately 21.5 million shares of Gold Royalty Corp. (NYSE American: GROY), 9.9 million shares of U.S. GoldMining Inc. (Nasdaq: USGO) and 19.1 million shares of NevGold Corp. (TSXV: NAU). See www.goldmining.com for additional information. For additional information, please contact: GoldMining Inc. title: Glass Lewis Recommends That Aurinia Shareholders Vote “FOR” All Proposals at 2025 Annual General Meeting
summary: ROCKVILLE, Md. & EDMONTON, Alberta--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Aurinia Pharmaceuticals Inc. (“Aurinia” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: AUPH) today announced that leading independent proxy advisor Glass, Lewis & Co. LLC (“Glass Lewis”) has recommended that Aurinia shareholders vote FOR all proposals put forth by the Board of Directors (the “Board”) at the Company’s 2025 Annual General Meeting (the “Meeting”) on Thursday, May 15, 2025, at 12:00 p.m., Eastern Time.
body_text: ROCKVILLE, Md. & EDMONTON, Alberta--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Aurinia Pharmaceuticals Inc. (“Aurinia” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: AUPH) today announced that leading independent proxy advisor Glass, Lewis & Co. LLC (“Glass Lewis”) has recommended that Aurinia shareholders vote FOR all proposals put forth by the Board of Directors (the “Board”) at the Company’s 2025 Annual General Meeting (the “Meeting”) on Thursday, May 15, 2025, at 12:00 p.m., Eastern Time. Glass Lewis supports all of the proposals in the Company’s proxy statement and management information circular (the “Proxy Statement/Circular”), including approving the six director nominees, the proposed auditor, the non-binding advisory vote on the Company’s approach to executive compensation, and an amendment to the Company’s Equity Incentive Plan. Shareholders of record at the close of business on April 12, 2025, are entitled to notice of, and to vote on the proposals described in the Proxy Statement/Circular. All votes must be received no later than 12:00 PM EST on May 13, 2025, to be counted for the Meeting. The proposals and details on how to vote are more fully described in the Proxy Statement/Circular, which can be found on the Company's profiles on EDGAR at www.sec.gov and SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca . About Aurinia Aurinia is a biopharmaceutical company focused on delivering therapies to people living with autoimmune diseases with high unmet medical needs. In January 2021, the Company introduced LUPKYNIS® (voclosporin), the first FDA-approved oral therapy for the treatment of adult patients with active lupus nephritis. Aurinia is also developing AUR200, a dual inhibitor of B cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation inducing ligand (APRIL) for the potential treatment of autoimmune diseases.

title: AI Calendar Scheduling for Founders: Cut the Back-and-Forth
summary: Stop the calendar ping-pong. This guide shows founders how to use AI calendar scheduling to automate availability, drafts, and prep directly in Gmail…
body_text: Most founders treat their calendar like a reactive game of Tetris. You wake up to three different threads asking for a quick sync and spend the next ninety minutes checking time zones, hunting for open slots, and sending links that the recipient ignores. This manual coordination is not just annoying: it is a high-cost leak of the most limited resource your startup has. The goal is a transition from being a manual gatekeeper to operating a system where scheduling is a background process. You need a setup where you never have to type 'does Thursday at 2pm work' again. By the end of this guide, you will have an email-native AI scheduling workflow that handles availability, booking, meeting prep, and reminders without leaving your inbox. This approach treats your time as a guarded asset rather than a public utility. You will achieve a state where meetings appear on your calendar with full context, zero manual data entry, and no chasing people down. Step 1: Audit Where Your Scheduling Time Actually Goes Founders lose approximately 6.2 hours every week to meeting coordination alone. This includes the time spent opening the calendar app, checking for conflicts, calculating time zone differences, and typing out availability options. (Slashy, 2026). This phenomenon is known as Logistics Debt. It is the invisible tax on your productivity that grows as your team and network expand. Start by tagging every email in your inbox from the last seven days that involves scheduling. Use a simple label like 'Scheduling' in Gmail. You will likely find that a single meeting takes an average of 3 to 5 emails to finalize. This back-and-forth creates a fragmented schedule often described as Swiss cheese: thirty-minute gaps between meetings that are too short for deep work but too long to ignore. Review these threads to identify the friction points. Are people ignoring your booking link? Are they asking for times you already told them were unavailable? Are you manually creating Zoom links and calendar invites? Slow scheduling responses often cause meetings to be delayed by several days, which creates a significant technical bottleneck for founders. Quantifying this delay helps you realize that scheduling is not a social task. It is a technical bottleneck. Once you see the hours lost, you can justify the move to an AI-native system. Step 2: Set Your Availability Rules Once (Not Per Email) A common mistake is treating your calendar as a blank slate for others to fill. AI calendar scheduling for founders requires hard boundaries that the system enforces automatically. You must define your 'Defensive Calendaring' rules. For example, you might decide that no external meetings happen before 11:00 AM or after 4:00 PM. Use a tool like Reclaim.ai to create smart habits and buffer times. Reclaim lets you set 'Decompression Breaks' that automatically appear after long meetings. If a meeting runs over, the AI shifts your subsequent availability to prevent a pile-up. You can compare different approaches to these rules in the Slashy vs Reclaim guide. Your rules should also include priority levels. Not every meeting deserves the same amount of your time. Set a rule that 'Investor' meetings can override 'Networking' blocks, but nothing overrides your 'Deep Work' sessions. When your AI system understands these constraints, it can offer times that protect your energy. This is a shift from static availability to dynamic scheduling. Your calendar should reflect your priorities, not just list your free time. Set these rules once and you eliminate the mental load of deciding whether you are 'actually' free every time an invite arrives. Step 3: Share a Booking Link That Knows Your Calendar Context Sending a raw booking link can feel dismissive to high-value contacts like investors or potential hires. It shifts the entire burden of work onto them. To solve this, use a context-aware booking system. Cal.com provides an open source infrastructure that allows for highly customizable scheduling links. The difference between a standard link and a context-aware link is 'Context Injection.' Instead of a generic URL, your AI system should generate a link that already knows who the recipient is and what the meeting is about. If you are using Slashy, the platform can automatically append metadata to the link so the booking page is personalized. This system also allows for 'Priority Routing.' If a high-priority lead clicks your link, they might see more available slots than a cold outbound prospect. You can also set links to expire. If someone does not book within 48 hours, the slot is released back to your general pool. This prevents 'Calendar Ghosting,' where people sit on your availability for days without committing. The booking link becomes an invitation to a frictionless experience rather than another task on the recipient's to-do list. Step 4: Let AI Draft the Scheduling Email for You The most efficient way to schedule is to never leave your inbox. Most founders toggle between Gmail and a calendar app forty times a day. An AI-native client like Slashy works like a 'Cursor for Email.' It reads the incoming request and drafts a reply that includes your available times directly in the text. This is called 'Inline Availability Injection.' Instead of saying 'here is my link,' the AI drafts: 'I would love to chat. I am free Thursday at 2:00 PM or Friday at 10:00 AM. If those do not work, you can see my full calendar here.' The AI pulls these slots based on the rules you set in Step 2. This creates a high-touch feel with zero manual effort. The AI can also detect the tone of the sender. If an email is formal, the draft will be formal. If it is a quick Slack-style message, the reply will be brief. This keeps your communication authentic while the AI handles the logistics. For a deeper look at how this works, read about the best Gmail AI assistant . When the AI handles the drafting, you move from being a typist to being an editor. You review the draft, hit send, and the meeting is effectively booked. Step 5: Automate Follow-Ups and No-Show Reminders Scheduling the meeting is only half the battle. Roughly 20% of founder meetings result in a no-show or a last-minute reschedule (Industry Data, 2026). This is often because the recipient lost the invite or forgot the context of the call. You must automate the 'Ghosting Protocol.' Your AI system should send a tiered series of reminders: a confirmation email immediately after booking, a reminder 24 hours before, and a soft nudge one hour before with the meeting link included. This reduces the friction for the guest. If the guest has not accepted the calendar invite within 24 hours of the meeting, the AI can trigger a polite follow-up asking if they need to reschedule. You can set these up using how to set up email follow-up reminders . The goal is to make sure the meeting actually happens once it is on the books. This automation also handles reschedules. If a guest clicks 'reschedule,' the AI should automatically offer new times based on your current availability, update the calendar invite, and notify you of the change. This removes you from the loop entirely until the actual meeting time arrives. Step 6: Generate Meeting Prep Before You Walk In Walking into a meeting cold is a waste of time. You end up spending the first ten minutes asking questions the guest already answered in their initial email. A truly intelligent inbox prepares you for the conversation. Before the meeting starts, your AI should generate a 'Contextual Briefing.' This briefing pulls from the last three emails, the contact's LinkedIn profile, and any relevant CRM data. It summarizes the goal of the meeting and identifies any pending 'asks' from either side. This is possible because of systems like The Email Client With a Memory System . Slashy uses this memory to make sure you never lose the thread of a conversation, even if it has been weeks since your last interaction. You should receive this briefing in your inbox or as a notification ten minutes before the call. It should include a list of 'Action Items' from previous threads. This makes you look prepared and respects the other person's time. Meeting prep is the final piece of the AI calendar scheduling for founders puzzle. It turns a calendar event into a productive business outcome. When the logistics and the preparation are both automated, you can focus entirely on the person in front of you. What to Do If the Back-and-Forth Keeps Happening Even with the best AI tools, some people will refuse to use a booking link or offer vague availability like 'sometime next week.' Do not let this break your system. When you encounter a 'Manual Scheduler,' use your AI to parse their text. If they say 'I am free Tuesday afternoon,' your AI client should instantly cross-reference that against your calendar and draft a reply that says 'Tuesday at 3:00 PM works perfectly. I have sent the invite.' If the back-and-forth continues beyond two emails, it is usually a sign of low intent. Use your AI to flag these threads as 'Low Priority.' You can then choose to batch these responses at the end of the day rather than letting them interrupt your focus. Some founders use a 'Gatekeeper AI' that requires external senders to provide a specific reason for the meeting before availability is shared. Finally, check your settings for 'Conflict Resolution.' Sometimes the back-and-forth happens because your AI is being too restrictive with your time. Adjust your 'Minimum Notice' and 'Buffer' settings until you find a balance that allows for spontaneity without sacrificing your deep work. You can learn more about managing these conflicts in the AI calendar guide . Scheduling is an iterative process. Refine your rules monthly based on which meetings actually provide value to your company. Conclusion The manual calendar is dying. Founders who keep spending five hours a week on scheduling logistics will be outpaced by those who treat their time as an automated asset. The classic 'booking link in signature' is no longer enough. It is too impersonal and too easy to ignore. By 2027, most professional meetings will be negotiated by background agents that understand context, priority, and personal energy levels. You can start building this system today. Stop fighting your inbox and start using a client that works for you. If you are ready to eliminate the scheduling ping-pong for good, sign up for Slashy and let the Intelligent Inbox handle your calendar. Spend your day building your company, not managing your invites.

title: Embryo Grading vs. Genetic Testing
summary: Embryo grades and genetic testing results answer different questions. Here is how to read them together without treating either one as the whole answer.
body_text: The same embryo can come back with two results. One says 4AA . The other says euploid . A different embryo might pair a modest 3BB with an aneuploid result. The two can seem to compete, as if one has to be the "real" grade. They are not competing. They answer two different questions about the same embryo. It helps to take them one at a time before you put them side by side. There are two separate things being measured. One is how the embryo looks as it grows. The other is what a few sampled cells tell the genetics lab . An embryo can score high on one and low on the other, which is exactly why the two results do not always agree. The rest of this article walks through each one on its own, then puts them side by side so the cases where they disagree make more sense. Grading: how the embryo looks as it grows Embryo grading is done by the embryology team, and it is essentially a visual and developmental assessment. At the blastocyst stage, many labs use a Gardner-style system that looks at three main features: how expanded the blastocyst is, how the inner cell mass appears, and how the trophectoderm appears. That is where a code like 4AA comes from: a number for expansion, then two letters for those two cell groups. The inner cell mass is the group of cells expected to contribute to the fetus. The trophectoderm is the outer layer expected to contribute to the placenta. ASRM's embryo grading materials describe these commonly used grading features, including Gardner-style expansion and cell-quality categories ( ASRM grading scales ). A higher grade often means the embryo looked more expanded or organized at the moment it was checked. That information can help a lab decide which embryos are suitable for biopsy, freezing, or transfer. But grade is a description, not a verdict. It is partly subjective. Two embryologists can score the same embryo a little differently, lab practices vary, and lower-graded embryos can still have real reproductive potential. The grade tells you how the embryo looked. It does not, by itself, say anything about chromosomes. Genetics: what the sampled cells show The second result comes from preimplantation genetic testing, or PGT, which usually involves removing a small number of cells from an embryo and sending those cells to a genetics laboratory. The grade looks at the whole embryo under a microscope; genetics looks only at the few cells that were sampled and asks one specific question of them. SART describes PGT as testing in which cells are removed from an embryo and screened for genetic abnormalities, with categories such as PGT-A , PGT-M , and PGT-SR ( SART glossary ). PGT-A Chromosome number Asks whether the sampled cells appear to have the expected number of chromosomes. PGT-M A known family variant Asks whether the embryo appears to have inherited a specific variant already identified in the family. PGT-SR A chromosome rearrangement Used when a parent carries a rearrangement that could lead to missing or extra chromosome material in embryos. For PGT-A, especially, cautious wording matters. ASRM notes that PGT-A use has grown, but that its value as routine screening for all IVF patients has not been demonstrated. SART also emphasizes that PGT-A is a screening test and does not guarantee an ongoing pregnancy or live birth ( ASRM 2024 committee opinion , SART FAQ ). Putting grade and genetics side by side Here is where grade and genetics come together. Because they are measured separately, every embryo falls into one of four boxes. Two boxes are the expected ones, where grade and genetics point the same way. The other two are the surprises, where a strong-looking embryo tests abnormal or a modest-looking one tests euploid. Those two boxes are the main reason it helps to compare grade and genetics at all. Euploid (expected chromosome number) Aneuploid (missing or extra chromosomes) Looks strong high grade Grade and genetics agree — the combination most people picture by default. The hard surprise. A great-looking embryo can still test aneuploid; appearance cannot see chromosome count. Looks modest lower grade The reassuring surprise. A modest-looking embryo can test euploid; a lower grade is not a chromosome problem, and it can still be considered for transfer. Grade and genetics agree the other way. Those two off-diagonal cases — a strong-looking embryo that tests aneuploid, and a modest-looking one that tests euploid — are why grade and genetics are not the same thing. Grade on its own does not decide whether an embryo becomes a healthy baby. A lower-graded euploid embryo can lead to a perfectly healthy pregnancy. But most full aneuploidies are unlikely to result in an ongoing, healthy pregnancy, which is why a chromosome finding usually carries more weight than appearance when the two disagree. If an embryo lands in one of those off-diagonal boxes, it does not mean either test failed. It means the embryo carries two kinds of information that do not have to match. The helpful question is not, "Which result should I ignore?" It is, "How does this clinic weigh these results for embryos like mine?" Policies can differ, especially for mosaic results, no-result embryos, day 7 embryos, or embryos with lower morphology grades. How clinics weigh grade and genetics together Even when embryos are genetically tested, grade still matters. Embryos first need to grow to a stage where the lab believes biopsy and freezing are appropriate, and that judgment leans on grade. After results return, the care team may consider the genetic result, embryo grade, day of blastocyst development, medical history, and patient priorities all at once. Question What helps answer it? Did the embryo look developmentally ready for biopsy, freezing, or transfer? Embryo grade and day of development Did the sampled cells appear to have the expected chromosome number? PGT-A result Was a known family variant or chromosome rearrangement part of the plan? PGT-M or PGT-SR result, if ordered What else could affect the chance of pregnancy? Age, uterus, medical history, embryo cohort, lab factors, and other clinical context This is why many clinic conversations sound layered. A clinician may talk about a euploid embryo with a lower grade, or a high-grade embryo that is not recommended for transfer because of a genetic result. Neither sentence is a contradiction. It means the team is reading both the grade and the genetics at once and deciding which one carries more weight for this specific embryo. A few questions worth asking How does this lab assign embryo grades, and how consistent is grading between embryologists? After PGT results are available, how much weight does embryo grade still carry? What result categories can this PGT lab report, such as mosaic, segmental, inconclusive, or no result? Would your recommendation change if we have one embryo, several embryos, recurrent pregnancy loss, advanced maternal age, or a known familial variant? What grade and genetics each add It is tempting to ask which result is the "real" one. But grade and genetics were never meant to give the same answer, so picking a winner does not help. A more useful question is: for this embryo and this decision, what does each one actually add? Grade tells you how the embryo developed and whether the lab considered it ready for the next step. Genetics tells you the answer to the specific question that was ordered of the sampled cells. Together, they describe an embryo more fully than either could alone. Neither one promises a pregnancy, a live birth, or a child without health conditions. One practical note: Reticular's report does not include embryo grade (morphology) by default. It focuses on the genetic layer. If grade matters to your decision, you can adjust your priorities and share the grading information so it is factored in.

title: Leadership Insights: A conversation with Seepika Singhal
summary: Explore Seepika Singhal’s inspiring HR journey across industries, as she shares insights on rewards, resilience, and reimagining employee experiences.
body_text: Seepika: The journey has been filled with twists and turns, and if I start with the beginning, I was born and brought up in a humble and grounded family setup. I never ever thought in my childhood that I would end up in HR as a profession. So I was good in studies, but I always wanted to prove myself in what I picked up, whether it was academics or co-curricular. So we were thirteen people cohabiting in one single household, and all the key decisions were taken by the head of the family, who used to be my grandfather, and those were my affirmative years. And I take a lot of pride in saying that I have imbibed all the values that have saved me today, the values of coexisting, adaptability, and respect that have come from the upbringing that I had. So there has been a continuous desire to prove myself and grow. And when I was in a small town, career services were very limited. So, being a good student, I had only two options that everyone expected me to do: either engineering or medicine. But I was kind of a challenger to that status quo. I wanted to do something different. I didn’t know at that time what difference it could make. But my parents trusted in me. I said that I want to be there where a lot of innovative and creative minds will be. So I wanted to come to Delhi University and do my graduation in humanities from here. And I pursued that despite everyone around me saying that toppers like you are not doing engineering or medicine, who else? Why are you not writing the engineering entrance examination? I said, no, I’m not interested in doing whatever everyone is doing. That’s not my cup of tea. I came with the mindset of doing civil services but eventually I saw towards the final years of my graduation that a career in management was something that attracted me more. I generally started to explore how admissions take place and all about it, and I appeared in all management exams and was admitted. And finally, I ended up taking admission in Sri Ram College of Commerce to do my master’s. So this was my educational journey, and this is a very interesting concept that I share with a few of my folks. I learned this concept of return on investment very early in my life. And I got admission in Narsee Monjee, Hyderabad, Amity Law School, and all these colleges. But I thought, let me see, what is the end outcome? So the line of sight was very clear to me. And I compared the statistics of placement. I saw that all these students who come out of these colleges end up in nearly similar companies and with similar packages. So I thought, I am investing in a college where the teachers, the kind of environment, the university environment, SRCC being the prestigious one, and at a very nominal fee. It was minuscule in comparison to what other colleges were charging, and also the travel and accommodation costs. I thought that if I ended up getting a package of similar lines, why invest more, so I thought of the return on my investment. I didn’t want it to end up where, from my first salary, I start giving EMIs. So I thought, let me do this, and then I was fortunate to be selected from the campus. I was one of the very first students who got campus placement at the beginning of the journey. Then HCL happened to be a very fulfilling 5 1/2 years of differentiated experience. In HCL Technologies, I got a lot of leadership positions, worked in multiple geographies, multiple assignments, and different roles. Then from there I moved to Capgemini. Capgemini was totally an international organization; from my IT pure play Indian company to Capgemini was completely different altogether. And the geography for me also was different. There I was taking care of North America as a compensation leader, and post-Capgemini again, I had fulfilling years of learning and delivering, and proved myself in that organization. Then I acquired the leadership position in Luminous Electric, where I was leading the rewards function. That was again kind of a challenge for me because from my IT setup company to manufacturing, dealing with blue-collar employees, white-collar employees, and Indian payroll and coming up with benefits, you have to think about policy, think about the blue-collar worker who’s able to understand that policy. So that was totally a challenge to me, which inspired me to take up that position, and I enjoyed that also. I seamlessly worked with the leaders and created differentiated rewards platforms and brought in experiential R&R practices at Luminous. So I was instrumental in bringing experience-based rewards in Luminous at that time. So from there, moving the employee EVP, working to an EVP in Luminous and then working in HT Media, which is totally a different company, very creative people, different talent mindset. From ST Media, I moved to R1 RCM, which was in healthcare and had a very huge presence in India as well as the US. So I had all these differentiated experiences. And then finally, I’m in video technologies, a very insurgent organization, with new ways of working on digital superpowers, CI, and dealing with very talented employees here. So I’m feeling grateful that whatever opportunities I have had in my career journey have made me what I am today. And I have learned from the leaders across geographies and a lot of industries, different industry segments that I worked in. And one thing that keeps me honest is that because the context is different, so one thing that you have created as a success in one company may not be replicated in another. So it always keeps you challenged, keeps you continuously engaged. And so, I keep reinventing myself with these talents.

title: Three data must-haves in applying GenAI to payments processing
summary: This CGI blog explores three data must-haves in applying GenAI to payments processing—data quality, alignment and governance.
body_text: A few years ago, I lived in a house in Toronto with a very common street name, Main Street. While the address was easy to remember, such a common name is often used as a “generic” or “fictional” address by people wanting to avoid junk mail being sent to their real addresses. This meant a lot of junk mail came rattling through my letterbox. In 2018, this situation took a more sinister turn when I started receiving letters and debit cards from a large Canadian bank with my address but a variety of names. Having reported this to a senior contact at the bank, I later found out this was part of an insider fraud scheme where thousands of fake accounts had been created, and a large investigation was required to address the problem. The bank was subsequently fined an exceptionally large sum by their regulator for failures that led to the fraud. The time it took to uncover the scheme, the money lost and laundered, and the subsequent fines imposed serve as a poignant example of the fiscal and reputational value of proactive data analytics, which could have revealed the issues much sooner. Publicly available information shows that the modest three-bedroom, semi-detached home at my address could realistically house a maximum of six adults. Likewise, it’s uncommon for every person in a household to have different family names. These are anomalies that trained AI-driven data analytics could have quickly identified in a database to ultimately avoid the fraudulent activity that took place. However, many banks are challenged in managing data and leveraging the full power of generative AI (GenAI), particularly in the payments space, to provide this proactive protection. Common issues include lack of data quality, alignment, and governance. Data quality: GenAI demands clean and compliant data Clearly, the starting point for getting the best out of GenAI tools in the payments space is improving data quality. While these tools can deliver a wealth of advantages, Marcus Martinez, FSI Industry Adviser at Microsoft, gave cautionary advice on its use during a CGI roundtable at EBAday 2024: “There's a huge concern with data quality. And, while I appreciate the whole hype around GenAI adoption, I think the industry is coming to the realization that, first and foremost, the data quality must be good before you start the journey.” Different organizations have different data cleansing approaches—some better than others. But the bottom line is that, before GenAI can be effectively applied and deliver the best results, data must be both clean and compliant. Data alignment: Fraud and right-to-be-forgotten challenges Payment service providers typically focus on maximizing straight-through processing (STP), which checks for affirmative answers to questions such as: Is this an account? Are there funds? Is there permission to send funds? The payment is then shuttled through screening and filtering processes to check if it’s fraudulent, non-compliant, or embargoed. This approach, however, can create potential fraud gaps because data checked as part of the STP processing isn’t always validated in the compliance process flow. As a result, the payment data is never examined holistically. Likewise, inbound and outbound payments are rarely compared, enabling problems to creep in. An inbound payment, if accepted, is generally stored “as is,” so in a payments database there may be multiple versions of customer records versus a single unified record. Not only does this create issues for traditional pattern checking, but it also makes the right-to-be-forgotten, mandated under Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) law, significantly more difficult for rule-based systems to deliver. ISO 20022 has been a big step toward achieving data alignment, particularly once structured address formats are adopted. Thanks to native systems such as CGI All Payments , the bulk of banks now store payment data in this rich format. However, rationalizing data and applications requires a better understanding of the payments data journey within an institution. This is yet another opportunity where GenAI tools can create complex mappings that simplify and unify data while driving efficiency. Data governance: Keeping humans in the loop Aligning payment recipient details for inbound payments with existing customer data makes it easier to synchronize and manage payment histories. If, at the same time, an AI bot runs anomaly and compliance checks on that inbound data, you can connect the dots more easily. Catching patterns that indicate your customer is a potential mule or part of a pool of fake accounts becomes much faster when those patterns are in line with acceptance and tied to internal or external data sources (e.g., land registries, electoral registers, and social media). However, as we implement GenAI tools, it’s important to maintain the right checks and balances to ensure that identified behavior patterns are verified before action is taken and that false positives are returned to the GenAI model so that it can improve. In short, we need to keep humans in the loop. During the CGI roundtable at EBAday 2024, Daniel Szmukler, Head of Innovation at the Euro Banking Association, explained, “I believe AI doesn’t stand for artificial intelligence when we’re talking about banking. It stands for augmented intelligence. We augment with automation and machine intelligence, but we can’t let the machine entirely take over the decision-making process.” The European Union strongly agrees with this view with its release of the recent EU Artificial Intelligence Act , which is designed to govern how this powerful technology can be used responsibly. In September 2024, CGI signed the EU’s AI Act Pledge as part of its engagement with the European Commission’s AI Pact. The signature reinforces CGI’s commitment globally to uphold the highest standards and best practices in the development and use of responsible technologies, including innovative AI and GenAI technologies. Advancing your GenAI journey through better data management The power of GenAI to transform payments processing is a reality. However, effective data management that ensures high-quality, aligned, and well-governed data across the enterprise is key to GenAI’s success. CGI is working with payment providers across the globe to create competitive advantage through GenAI. To learn more about our work, feel free to contact me or visit cgi.com .

title: Arbor Summer Interns Learn About the Lifecycle of a Loan and Much More
summary: Arbor’s summer interns are a key part of our ongoing initiative to nurture talent and shape future leaders through programs.
body_text: Arbor’s summer internship program is a key part of our ongoing initiative to nurture talent and shape future leaders through programs, such as Fannie Mae’s DUS® Summer Series, and networking opportunities. DUS® Summer Series Educates Interns on the Life of a Loan Fannie Mae’s DUS Summer Series, an annual webinar open to employees of DUS lenders like Arbor, is designed to provide education about the broader commercial mortgage industry, Fannie Mae, and its DUS program , while helping participants become aware of opportunities in the multifamily sector. Arbor has played a key role in developing the program, which is available to summer interns and early-career employees, including those who have been with a company for less than one year or have recently transitioned to the multifamily sector. Interns and Employees Reflect on the Summer Series Tracy Dennis , Managing Director, General Counsel, Agency and Arbor Private Label at Arbor: “This year, we added a career panel for one of the sessions that included professionals who were in different stages of their careers. We wanted to make sure that the participants could better relate to the professionals, which is why we also made sure to include people who are earlier in their careers.” Marisa Mamak , Marketing intern: “One of the key takeaways I gained from the DUS Operation Summer Speaker Series is skills for my post-grad life. Speakers in the weekly seminar emphasized the importance of taking initiative and having the willingness to learn. Companies seek individuals who can demonstrate leadership and are eager to grow and develop.” Jake Borgese , Agency Production intern: “Hearing from professionals across production, underwriting, and other areas has given me a broader perspective on how each position contributes to the loan process and has helped me better understand where I can continue to grow professionally.” Building a Strong Foundation in CRE Finance Regardless of the department, Arbor strives to emphasize the importance of growing long-term partnerships, both with our clients and our colleagues. It is a philosophy that extends to all departments, employees, and tasks. Andrew Maiella , Screening intern: “I’ve gotten to the point where I am screening my own deals that come into my team’s queue, including working with an analyst on screening and quoting two separate 15+ unit portfolios. This is my first internship, so all of it was new when I started, but the biggest thing I’ve taken away is what kills a deal early in screening.” Ryan DeSimone , Capital Markets intern: “By building different models from scratch this summer, I gained a fundamental understanding of the core differences between Freddie and Fannie pricing and learned how j-spread models draw from active U.S. Treasury curves to adjust to market fluctuations.” Arbor Colleagues Pay It Forward Arbor is proud that several colleagues have served as intern mentors over the years, supporting students as they build connections in commercial real estate and helping drive Arbor’s continued growth. Ryan Kraynak , Vice President, Screening, who is working with four interns this summer, said that he always treats aspiring professionals as if they were new full-time hires. “I pair interns with analysts in a training program to help them navigate their workbooks, which I’ve found is a more meaningful experience for them,” said Kraynak. “Working with interns for several years has reinforced things that I already knew: that these students are hungry to learn and ready to make an impact.” Developing Future Talent at Arbor Kraynak said he’s had interns return to spend another summer at Arbor, and some have been hired full-time. Joseph Hayek , a Payment Processing intern in Arbor’s Buffalo office this summer, recently accepted a full-time Portfolio Analyst I role in our Portfolio Management department. “From my first day as an Intern, every question I asked was met with timely, thoughtful guidance, making it easy to learn and grow with confidence,” said Hayek. “The willingness of colleagues to help and collaborate has created an environment where I never hesitate to seek advice or expand my knowledge.” Anna Weiss Cohen , Screening and Production Management intern, is in her second summer interning at Arbor. “I came back because I wanted the chance to see a different side of the lending process,” said Cohen. “Last year, I was on the asset management side, tracking loan performance and doing site visits after deals closed.” “This summer, I moved into screening and production and got exposure to a deal from initial underwriting through credit approval,” she said. “Getting to see both sides of the loan life cycle has helped me build a more complete understanding of the business.” Visit our Careers page for more information about working at Arbor and to stay updated on job opportunities.
